questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Whether the period of a spring–mass oscillator and of a simple pendulum change on the Moon
questions.question: A spring–mass oscillator and a simple pendulum each have a period of 1.0 s on the Earth. Both are taken to the Moon, where g is one-sixth of its value on the Earth. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The spring–mass period stays 1.0 s (it does not depend on g, whether the spring is horizontal or vertical), while the pendulum period becomes about 2.4 s
B) Both periods become about 2.4 s
C) The spring–mass period becomes about 2.4 s and the pendulum period stays 1.0 s
D) Both periods become about 0.41 s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The spring–mass period stays 1.0 s; the pendulum period becomes about 2.4 s.
Given: \(T_{\text{spring}}=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\ T_{\text{pendulum}}=2\pi\sqrt{L/g};\ g_{\text{Moon}}=g/6\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{restoring force: spring }-kx\ (\text{no g});\ \text{pendulum }-mg\theta\ (\text{depends on g})\)
Step 1: \(\text{vertical spring: g only shifts the equilibrium position (extension }mg/k)\text{, not the period}\)
Step 2: \(T_{\text{pendulum}}\propto\dfrac1{\sqrt g}\Rightarrow T'=1.0\times\sqrt6\)
Worked derivation: \[T'_{\text{pendulum}}=\sqrt6\ \mathrm s\approx2.45\ \mathrm s;\qquad T'_{\text{spring}}=1.0\ \mathrm s\]
Check: \[\text{about the new equilibrium: }m\ddot y=-ky\text{ for a vertical spring, independent of g}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{for a spring the restoring force comes from elasticity; for a pendulum it comes from gravity}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the spring–mass period does not depend on g}\); (C) \(\text{reverses the two cases}\); (D) \(\text{a smaller g lengthens the pendulum period; it does not shorten it}\).
Key point: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\ (\text{g-independent});\ T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Wave speed, frequency, wavelength and maximum particle speed from a progressive wave equation
questions.question: A transverse wave on a string is described by \(y=0.030\sin\left[\pi(40t-0.50x)\right]\), with x and y in metres and t in seconds. What are the wave speed and its direction, the frequency, the wavelength and the maximum speed of a particle of the string?
options: A) 20 m s⁻¹ in −x direction; 40 Hz; 2.0 m; 1.2 m s⁻¹
B) 80 m s⁻¹ in −x direction; 20 Hz; 4.0 m; 3.8 m s⁻¹
C) 80 m s⁻¹ in +x direction; 20 Hz; 4.0 m; about 3.8 m s⁻¹
D) 0.0125 m s⁻¹ in +x direction; 40 Hz; 0.50 m; 1.2 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 80 m s⁻¹ along +x; 20 Hz; 4.0 m; about 3.8 m s⁻¹.
Given: \(y=A\sin(\omega t-kx),\ A=0.030\ \mathrm m,\ \omega=40\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\ k=0.50\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,m^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\dfrac\omega k,\ f=\dfrac\omega{2\pi},\ \lambda=\dfrac{2\pi}k,\ v_{\text{particle,max}}=A\omega;\ (\omega t-kx)\Rightarrow\text{travels along }+x\)
Step 1: \(v=\dfrac{40\pi}{0.50\pi}=80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\ f=\dfrac{40\pi}{2\pi}=20\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda=\dfrac{2\pi}{0.50\pi}=4.0\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[v_{\max}=A\omega=0.030\times40\pi=1.2\pi\approx3.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[v=f\lambda=20\times4.0=80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a fixed phase }40t-0.5x=\text{const requires x to increase as t increases}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reads 40 as the frequency and 0.5 as }2\pi/\lambda\text{ without the factor }\pi\); (B) \(\text{a }(\omega t-kx)\text{ wave travels along }+x\text{, not }-x\); (D) \(\text{divides k by }\omega\text{ instead of }\omega\text{ by k}\).
Key point: \(y=A\sin(\omega t-kx):\ v=\omega/k\ \text{along }+x;\ \text{particle speed max}=A\omega\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Shape of the graph of the electric field on the axis of a uniformly charged ring
questions.question: A thin ring of radius R carries a uniformly distributed positive charge Q. Which description fits the graph of the axial field component E against the distance x along the axis from the centre (x positive on one side, negative on the other)?
options: A) E is greatest at the centre and falls steadily with distance on both sides

B) E is zero at the centre, rises to a maximum at \(x=R/\sqrt2\), then falls off roughly as \(1/x^2\) at large distances; on the other side E has the same shape but points the opposite way (negative values)
C) E is constant along the axis, like the field of an infinite sheet
D) E is zero at the centre and keeps increasing with distance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zero at the centre, maximum at \(x=R/\sqrt2\), then \(\approx1/x^2\); reversed in sign on the other side.
Given: \(\text{ring of radius }R,\ \text{charge }Q\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_x=\dfrac{kQx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}\ (\text{perpendicular components cancel by symmetry})\)
Step 1: \(x=0:\ E=0\ (\text{contributions from opposite points cancel})\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dE}{dx}\propto(R^2+x^2)-3x^2=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}\)
Worked derivation: \[x\gg R:\ E\approx\frac{kQ}{x^2};\qquad E(-x)=-E(x)\ (\text{odd function})\]
Check: \[E_{\max}=\frac{kQ(R/\sqrt2)}{(3R^2/2)^{3/2}}=\frac{2kQ}{3\sqrt3R^2}\approx0.385\frac{kQ}{R^2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{close to the centre the field is weak by symmetry; far away the ring looks like a point charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the field at the centre is zero, not greatest}\); (C) \(\text{a finite ring is not an infinite sheet; its field depends on x}\); (D) \(\text{far away the field must fall off as for a point charge}\).
Key point: \(\text{ring: }E=kQx/(R^2+x^2)^{3/2},\ \max\text{ at }R/\sqrt2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Potential energy of three equal charges at the corners of an equilateral triangle and the work to halve the side
questions.question: Three point charges, each +1.0 µC, are held at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.30 m. What is the electrostatic potential energy of the system, and how much work must an external agent do to move them slowly to the corners of a triangle of side 0.15 m? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
options: C) 0.090 J; zero, because the charges stay on an equipotential surface
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.090 J; 0.090 J.
Given: \(q=1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm C,\ a=0.30\ \mathrm m\to0.15\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=k\sum_{\text{pairs}}\dfrac{q_iq_j}{r_{ij}}=\dfrac{3kq^2}{a}\ (\text{three pairs});\ W_{\text{ext}}=\Delta U\)
Step 1: \(U_1=\dfrac{3\times9.0\times10^9\times10^{-12}}{0.30}=0.090\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(U\propto\dfrac1a\Rightarrow U_2=2U_1=0.18\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{\text{ext}}=U_2-U_1=0.18-0.090=0.090\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\text{each pair: }\frac{kq^2}{a}=\frac{9\times10^{-3}}{0.30}=0.030\ \mathrm J;\ 3\text{ pairs}=0.090\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{like charges repel, so pushing them closer needs positive work, which is stored as potential energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts only one pair}\); (B) \(\text{gives the final energy, not the change}\); (C) \(\text{moving the charges closer changes their potential energy; they do not move along an equipotential}\).
Key point: \(U=k\sum q_iq_j/r_{ij};\ \text{halving all distances doubles U}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Deflection of a compass needle at the centre of a current-carrying coil set in the magnetic meridian
questions.question: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm is set with its plane in the magnetic meridian, and a small compass needle is placed at its centre. A current of 0.10 A is passed through the coil. The horizontal component of the Earth's field is 3.14 × 10⁻⁵ T. What is the deflection of the needle, and what would it be if the current were doubled? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
options: A) 45°; about 63°
D) 63°; about 76°
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 45°; about 63°.
Given: \(N=50,\ R=0.10\ \mathrm m,\ I=0.10\ \mathrm A,\ B_H=3.14\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Biot–Savart law for a circular coil: }B=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}\text{ at the centre, perpendicular to the coil (and so to }B_H);\ \tan\theta=\dfrac{B}{B_H}\)
Step 1: \(B=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times50\times0.10}{2\times0.10}=\pi\times10^{-5}=3.14\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T\)
Step 2: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{3.14\times10^{-5}}{3.14\times10^{-5}}=1\Rightarrow\theta=45^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[I\to0.20\ \mathrm A:\ \tan\theta'=2\Rightarrow\theta'=63.4^\circ\]
Check: \[\text{deflection is not proportional to current: doubling I doubles }\tan\theta,\text{ not }\theta\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the needle aligns with the resultant of two perpendicular fields: the coil's field and the Earth's horizontal field}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{assumes }\theta\propto I\); (C) \(\text{uses }\mu_0NI/(4R)\text{ or forgets N partly}\); (D) \(\text{uses the diameter in place of the radius (doubling B)}\).
Key point: \(B=\mu_0NI/2R;\ \tan\theta=B/B_H\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Self-inductance of a long solenoid, energy stored, and the induced emf when the current changes
questions.question: A long air-cored solenoid has 1000 turns, length 0.50 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻³ m². What is its self-inductance, how much energy does it store at a current of 2.0 A, and what emf is induced if this current falls uniformly to zero in 0.010 s? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.5 mH; 5.0 mJ; 0.50 V.
Given: \(N=1000,\ l=0.50\ \mathrm m,\ A=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2},\ I=2.0\ \mathrm A,\ \Delta t=0.010\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(L=\dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l};\ U=\tfrac12LI^2;\ \varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(L=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10^6\times10^{-3}}{0.50}=2.51\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm H\)
Step 2: \(U=\tfrac12\times2.51\times10^{-3}\times4.0=5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[|\varepsilon|=L\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}=2.51\times10^{-3}\times\frac{2.0}{0.010}=0.50\ \mathrm V\]
Check: \[\text{flux linkage }N\Phi=LI=5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Wb};\ \text{change in 0.010 s}\Rightarrow0.50\ \mathrm V\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the induced emf opposes the fall in current (Lenz's law), trying to keep it flowing}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }\mu_0N^2A/(2l)\); (B) \(\text{omits the factor }\tfrac12\text{ in the energy}\); (D) \(\text{drops the factor }10^{-3}\text{ from the area}\).
Key point: \(L=\mu_0N^2A/l;\ U=\tfrac12LI^2;\ \varepsilon=L\,\Delta I/\Delta t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Current, voltages across L and C, and power factor of a series LCR circuit at resonance
questions.question: A series circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.10 H and C = 10 µF, connected to a 20 V (rms) a.c. source whose angular frequency can be varied. Which statement about the circuit at resonance is correct?
options: A) Resonance occurs at ω = 100 rad s⁻¹ and the current is 0.20 A
B) At resonance the impedance is greatest, so the current is least
C) At resonance the voltage across the inductor can never exceed the source voltage

D) Resonance occurs at ω = 1000 rad s⁻¹; the impedance equals R, so the rms current is 2.0 A and the power factor is 1; the rms voltages across L and across C are each 200 V, ten times the source voltage, but they cancel each other
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ω₀ = 1000 rad s⁻¹; Z = R; I = 2.0 A; power factor 1; V_L = V_C = 200 V, cancelling.
Given: \(R=10\ \Omega,\ L=0.10\ \mathrm H,\ C=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm F,\ V=20\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2};\ \text{resonance: }X_L=X_C,\ \omega_0=\dfrac1{\sqrt{LC}}\)
Step 1: \(\omega_0=\dfrac1{\sqrt{0.10\times1.0\times10^{-5}}}=\dfrac1{10^{-3}}=1000\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(Z=R=10\ \Omega\Rightarrow I=\dfrac{20}{10}=2.0\ \mathrm A;\ \cos\phi=\dfrac RZ=1\)
Worked derivation: \[X_L=\omega_0L=100\ \Omega\Rightarrow V_L=IX_L=200\ \mathrm V=V_C\ (\text{opposite phase})\]
Check: \[Q=\frac{\omega_0L}{R}=10=\frac{V_L}{V}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only R; the large equal and opposite voltages across L and C add to zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }\omega_0=1/(LC)\text{ or similar; the correct value is }1/\sqrt{LC}\); (B) \(\text{impedance is least at resonance, so the current is greatest}\); (C) \(V_L=QV\text{ can be much larger than V when }Q>1\).
Key point: \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC};\ Z=R;\ V_L=V_C=QV\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Radius of the circle of light escaping from a point source under water, and how it scales with depth
questions.question: A small lamp is placed 2.0 m below the surface of still water (refractive index 4/3). Light from it escapes only through a circular patch of the surface. What is the radius of this patch, and by what factor does its area change if the lamp is moved to a depth of 4.0 m?
options: A) About 1.5 m; area doubles
B) About 2.3 m; area becomes 4 times
C) About 2.7 m; area becomes 4 times
D) About 2.3 m; area doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 2.3 m; the area becomes 4 times.
Given: \(h=2.0\ \mathrm m,\ n=\tfrac43\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{total internal reflection beyond the critical angle: }\sin C=\dfrac1n;\ r=h\tan C=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{n^2-1}}\)
Step 1: \(\sin C=\tfrac34;\ \tan C=\dfrac{3/4}{\sqrt{1-9/16}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt7}\)
Step 2: \(r=2.0\times\dfrac{3}{\sqrt7}=\dfrac{6}{2.646}\approx2.27\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[r\propto h\Rightarrow\text{area}=\pi r^2\propto h^2:\ \left(\frac{4.0}{2.0}\right)^2=4\]
Check: \[\sqrt{n^2-1}=\sqrt{16/9-1}=\sqrt7/3\Rightarrow r=\frac{3h}{\sqrt7}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{rays hitting the surface at more than the critical angle are totally internally reflected, so only a cone of half-angle C escapes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }r=h\sin C\text{ and assumes the area scales with h}\); (C) \(\text{uses }r=h/\cos C\text{ (the slant distance)}\); (D) \(\text{radius right, but area scales as }r^2\).
Key point: \(r=h/\sqrt{n^2-1};\ \text{area}\propto h^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction and how it changes with slit width and wavelength
questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a single slit 0.20 mm wide, and the pattern is seen on a screen 1.0 m away. What is the width of the central bright band? What does it become (i) if the slit width is halved, and (ii) if blue light of 450 nm is used with the original slit?
options: C) 6.0 mm; (i) 12 mm; (ii) 4.5 mm
D) 6.0 mm; (i) 12 mm; (ii) 8.0 mm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6.0 mm; (i) 12 mm; (ii) 4.5 mm.
Given: \(\lambda=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m,\ a=2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm m,\ D=1.0\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{first minima at }a\sin\theta=\pm\lambda;\ \text{central width}=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\ (\text{small angles})\)
Step 1: \(w=\dfrac{2\times6.0\times10^{-7}\times1.0}{2.0\times10^{-4}}=6.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(w\propto\dfrac1a:\ a\to\tfrac a2\Rightarrow w=12\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Worked derivation: \[w\propto\lambda:\ w=6.0\times\frac{450}{600}=4.5\ \mathrm{mm}\]
Check: \[\theta=\lambda/a=3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}\ (\text{small, so the approximation holds})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a narrower slit spreads light more; shorter wavelengths spread less}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }\lambda D/a\text{ (half-width) and reverses both dependences}\); (B) \(\text{reverses both dependences}\); (D) \(\text{reverses the wavelength dependence}\).
Key point: \(\text{central maximum width}=2\lambda D/a\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the energy of a photon and the kinetic energy of an electron with the same wavelength of 1 nm
questions.question: A photon and an electron each have a wavelength of 1.0 nm. How do their momenta compare, and what are the photon energy and the electron kinetic energy? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; hc = 1240 eV nm)
options: A) Equal momenta; photon about 1240 eV; electron about 1.5 eV
B) Equal momenta; both about 1240 eV
C) The electron has the larger momentum; photon about 1240 eV; electron about 1.5 eV
D) Equal momenta; photon about 1.5 eV; electron about 1240 eV
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Equal momenta; photon ≈ 1240 eV; electron ≈ 1.5 eV.
Given: \(\lambda=1.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{de Broglie: }p=\dfrac h\lambda\text{ for both};\ E_{\text{photon}}=pc;\ K_{\text{electron}}=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}\)
Step 1: \(p=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{1.0\times10^{-9}}=6.63\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\ (\text{same for both})\)
Step 2: \(E_{\text{photon}}=\dfrac{hc}\lambda=\dfrac{1240}{1.0}=1240\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Worked derivation: \[K_e=\frac{p^2}{2m_e}=\frac{(6.63\times10^{-25})^2}{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}}=2.41\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J\approx1.5\ \mathrm{eV}\]
Check: \[\lambda(\mathrm{nm})\approx\frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\Rightarrow V=1.227^2\approx1.5\ \mathrm V\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the same wavelength means the same momentum, but energy depends on momentum differently: linearly for a photon, quadratically (and divided by 2m) for a slow electron}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }E=pc\text{ for the electron, which applies only to massless particles}\); (C) \(p=h/\lambda\text{ gives equal momenta for equal wavelengths}\); (D) \(\text{swaps the two energies}\).
Key point: \(\text{same }\lambda\Rightarrow\text{same }p;\ E_\gamma=pc\gg K_e=p^2/2m\)
